opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one we worried about a lot. Whenever you use an LLM as a judge, you're introducing a second model with its own blind spots into the measurement, so you have to ask whether what you're seeing is a property of the system under test or of the evaluator.

A few things gave us some comfort. First, the core finding wasn't subtle. When we compared the same models with and without retrieval, the shift in behavior was large and consistent. Models that would refuse a harmful request on their own became noticeably more willing to comply once you gave them retrieved documents, even fairly benign ones. A judge bias would have to be very specifically shaped, triggered by the presence of retrieved context, to manufacture that kind of difference. Since we used the same judge across conditions, a lot of the generic bias washes out in the comparison.

Second, we validated the judge against human annotations on a sample, and we looked closely at where they disagreed. That's where you learn the most. Judges tend to be a bit literal. They can be swayed by a disclaimer at the top of a response, or they can penalize a long answer that's mostly safe but has one problematic sentence buried in it. Those are real failure modes, and they mean I wouldn't put a lot of weight on precise absolute numbers, like exactly what percentage of responses were unsafe.

So my framing is this. The direction and rough magnitude of the effect are robust. The fine-grained rankings, say model A being slightly safer than model B in the RAG setting, are where judge bias could plausibly flip a conclusion, and I'd treat those more cautiously.

More broadly, I think this is a field-wide issue. We're increasingly evaluating safety with models that were themselves trained with particular notions of what's safe, and those notions may not match a specific deployment context. A financial services company, for example, has very particular concerns that a general-purpose judge won't capture. So part of the message of the work is that you need domain-specific taxonomies and some human grounding. An off-the-shelf judge is a useful instrument, but you shouldn't treat it as ground truth.

r001.rationale: The response says the behavioral shift was large and consistent, but it does not state that the compared rates differed by orders of magnitude or use such a gap to support robustness.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question we worried about a lot, and I think it's the right one to ask, because our headline finding is really dependent on the judge. Just to recap for listeners: we took a bunch of models that are, you know, pretty well aligned out of the box, and we found that when you put them in a RAG setup, so you retrieve documents and stuff them in the context, they become less safe. They'll answer questions they would have refused without retrieval, and the retrieved documents don't even need to be unsafe themselves for that to happen. And the way we measure "less safe" is largely with an LLM judge that looks at the response and classifies it as safe or unsafe, sometimes with a finer-grained taxonomy.

So there are a few ways the judge's bias could creep in. The most obvious one is length and verbosity. RAG responses tend to be longer, they tend to cite things, they have this authoritative tone. And we know LLM judges, like people, are susceptible to that. A longer, more confident answer can get rated as more harmful simply because it looks like it's "really answering," even if the actual informational content isn't more dangerous than a shorter response. The flip side is also possible: a judge might see a response that's hedged and full of "according to the document" language and be more lenient toward it, because it reads as grounded rather than as the model volunteering harmful content.

The second concern is that the judge shares a world model with the models being judged. If we use a frontier model as the judge, and it has its own idea of what counts as a harmful topic, that idea is going to be baked into every label. So when we say "model X is unsafe 30 percent of the time in the finance domain," what we're really saying is that it's unsafe according to one particular model's opinion of what finance harm looks like. That's a real limitation, and it's one of the reasons we were careful to say the study is about the relative change. The direction of the effect, retrieval makes things worse, that held up across judges and across our human spot checks. The absolute numbers I'd put much less weight on.

What we did to mitigate this: we ran a human annotation on a sample and measured agreement, and the agreement was good but not perfect. We also tried to be more precise in how we defined the categories, because a lot of the judge disagreement with humans came from genuinely ambiguous cases, things like a question about tax rules where it's unclear if the answer is advice or just information. So it wasn't that the judge was random, it was that the construct itself is fuzzy at the boundaries. And honestly, I think that's a lesson that goes beyond our paper. If you're going to use an LLM as a judge for safety, the first thing you should be checking isn't whether the judge is accurate, it's whether your definition of unsafe is crisp enough that two humans would agree. If humans don't agree, the judge can't be right in any meaningful sense.

So, to answer directly: I think bias in the judge could inflate or deflate the magnitude of what we report, and it probably affects some domains more than others. But I don't think it explains the core result away, because the result is a consistent gap between the same model with and without retrieval, under the same judge, and we see that gap in the human-labeled subset too. If anything, the experience made me more skeptical of any safety benchmark that reports a single number from a single judge without that kind of validation.

r001.rationale: The response says the relative effect held across judges and appeared in human-labeled examples, but it does not cite an orders-of-magnitude difference between the compared rates as the reason the finding is robust.

astra-6.text:
I think it limits how strongly we can interpret the results. If we use an LLM to judge whether a RAG response is safe, we’re measuring safety through that model’s particular preferences and blind spots. It might reward a response that sounds cautious while missing harmful content, or flag a legitimate answer because it discusses a sensitive topic.

For comparisons, the key question is whether that bias affects the systems equally. If the judge favors a style that one system produces more often, an apparent safety improvement could partly be a judging artifact. Using the same judge across systems doesn’t automatically solve that.

So I’d frame the conclusions as evidence under a particular evaluation setup, rather than an absolute statement that a system is safe. Human review and checks with different judges would help establish whether the findings hold up. Without those checks, that uncertainty needs to remain part of the conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention an orders-of-magnitude difference or argue that it makes the main finding robust. It instead says judge bias could affect comparisons and that conclusions need qualification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key concern is that an LLM judge gives us a measurement of safety, and that measurement can itself be biased. It might respond to the style of an answer—whether it sounds cautious, for example—without reliably determining whether the answer actually contains harmful information. If RAG changes that style, the judge could interpret that as a change in safety.

So I would distinguish between saying, “The judge rates this condition as safer,” and saying, “This condition is safer.” Even using the same judge across conditions doesn’t eliminate the issue, because its biases might affect those conditions differently. You’d want to check whether the conclusions hold with human judgments and other evaluators. Without that, I’d treat the findings as evidence under a particular evaluation setup, rather than a definitive statement about RAG safety.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention an orders-of-magnitude difference between rates or argue that this makes the study’s main finding robust. It instead says judge bias could affect conditions differently and treats the findings as provisional without other evaluations.
